claims.text: High configurational entropy governs the high-temperature stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Differences among constituent elements' atomic diffusion barriers govern nanoparticle stability.
When thermal energy overcomes the diffusion barriers of relatively mobile elements, those elements segregate from the random solid solution.
Elemental segregation causes local phase separation and loss of structural and chemical stability.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneously mixed, near-equiatomic solid solutions.
Reducing the concentration of elements with lower diffusion barriers will increase the nanoparticles' overall resistance to diffusion.
Elemental homogeneity and stability at grain boundaries mediate diffusion and surface segregation.
High configurational entropy in the as-synthesized nanoparticles retards atomic mobility and diffusion under moderate conditions.
Constituent elements have different effective kinetic barriers to migration at elevated temperature and in reactive atmospheres.
Elements with lower diffusion barriers preferentially migrate and cause local elemental segregation.

Modified nanoparticles containing less of the low-diffusion-barrier elements will exhibit less elemental segregation than the standard nanoparticles under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The modified nanoparticles will retain a more homogeneous phase structure than the standard nanoparticles.
Greater retention of phase homogeneity will produce more stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The proposed mechanism dominates only above a critical temperature at which relevant kinetic barriers are overcome.
The proposed mechanism is primarily applicable under reactive, oxidative atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in inert atmospheres or at lower temperatures where diffusion is negligible.
Nanoparticle size and morphology can affect diffusion kinetics.
Comparable segregation and phase changes in the modified and standard batches under identical conditions would falsify the proposed diffusion-barrier explanation.
